hero.name: Rekha
hero.who: a 52-year-old vice-principal in Bhopal who is quick to judge students who misbehave

story.b: Rekha has been vice-principal of a large school in Bhopal for six years. Outside her office is a wooden bench where students in trouble wait. Today two Class 9 boys sit there. During lunch, Devansh shoved another boy so hard into the water cooler that its tap broke. Rekha knows Devansh well. He has been in trouble since Class 6. She writes aggressive, repeat offender in the register and calls his parents for a meeting. That evening, over tea, her own daughter asks a simple question. Why did he push the boy? Rekha opens her mouth and realises she does not know. She never asked. She just knew what kind of boy he was.

ask.q: Rekha has already labelled the boy aggressive. What should she do before deciding on a punishment?
o: Find out what was going on for the boy before and around the fight
Give the harshest punishment so others learn a lesson
Go by his past record, since it shows who he really is
ask.why: A label explains nothing and stops her from looking further. Harsh punishment without understanding may teach fear but not change behaviour. A past record shows a pattern but not its causes. Asking what led to the fight gives her something she can work with.

chapters.take: A label is not an explanation. Ask what led to the behaviour.

story.b: The next morning Rekha calls Devansh in alone and, for the first time, simply asks. It takes a while for him to talk. The story comes out in pieces. His family shares one room, and his father works night shifts, so sleep is broken and noisy. He skipped breakfast. The other boy had been mocking his stammer for weeks in front of the girls. At home, shouting and slamming doors is how arguments usually go. And that morning he had got back a maths test with very low marks. Rekha writes each piece on her notepad. None of them alone explains the shove. Together, they explain a lot more than her one word did.

ask.q: A teacher complains that a Class 7 girl has suddenly stopped doing homework. What should Rekha do?
o: Conclude the girl has become lazy and call her parents
Blame her mobile phone, since that is the usual reason
Look for several possible reasons, like sleep, home, friends and health, before deciding
ask.why: Laziness and phones are single, easy explanations that may miss the real story. Behaviour usually grows from many causes working together, from tiredness to trouble at home or with friends. Looking across several layers gives a fairer picture and a better chance of helping her.

chapters.take: Behaviour rarely has one cause. Look across many layers before judging.

story.b: In a staff meeting, a teacher complains about Kabir from Class 5. He cannot sit still, fidgets, drops things. She says some children are simply born naughty. Rekha decides to watch Kabir through one full day. In the hot, crowded classroom, squeezed onto the last bench, he is restless and fiddly. In the drawing class held under the gulmohar tree, he is calm and focused for forty minutes. In the science lab, where he can move between tables, he asks the best questions. Same boy, very different behaviour. Rekha moves him to a front seat near the window, and his class teacher starts giving him small errands between lessons. Within weeks the complaints become rare.

ask.q: A teacher says a restless boy is just born that way and nothing will change. What is the best reply?
o: Agree, since some children are simply wired to misbehave
Explain that his nature and his setting work together, so changing the setting may help
Disagree, since behaviour comes only from how children are raised
ask.why: Saying it is all nature or all upbringing misses how the two shape each other. The same child can struggle in a hot, cramped room and thrive in a calm, open one. Seeing both lets the school change what it can, like seating and short breaks.

chapters.take: Nature and setting work together. Change the setting, and behaviour can change.

story.b: Every year, the Hindi-medium and English-medium sections of Class 8 mock each other. This year it gets worse. Before the annual function, someone tears a poster made by the other section, and both sides blame each other in the corridor. Rekha considers keeping the sections apart, but she knows that only hardens the line. Instead, for the science exhibition, she creates mixed teams of six, three from each section, each building one working model. At first the teams sit in two halves. By the second week, a Hindi-medium girl is explaining circuits while an English-medium boy writes the chart. On exhibition day, the best model comes from a mixed team, and both sections cheer for it.

ask.q: The Hindi-medium and English-medium sections mock each other at every event. Which step would ease it best?
o: Put students from both sections on mixed teams with a shared goal
Keep the sections apart so they cannot clash
Lecture both sections about respect in the assembly
ask.why: Group lines form fast and quietly, but they are flexible. Keeping groups apart lets the divide harden, and lectures rarely change gut feelings. Working together on a shared goal blurs the line, because teammates stop seeing each other as the other side.

chapters.take: Us and them lines are flexible. Shared goals help blur them.

story.b: A maths teacher storms into Rekha's office. Ishita from Class 10 shouted at him in front of the whole class. Rekha's first reaction is anger. Then she asks what happened just before. The teacher had been reading out every student's marks aloud, and Ishita's closest friend, who had failed, was crying at her desk. Ishita stood up and shouted at him to stop. Rekha thinks about it. If Ishita had shouted to stop a bully on the school bus, she would have praised her courage. The act is the same. The situation is different. Rekha talks to both. Ishita apologises for her tone, and the teacher agrees to stop reading marks aloud in class.

ask.q: Rekha hears that a quiet boy shoved an older student on the school bus. What should she ask first?
o: Which rule the boy broke, so the punishment matches
Whether the boy has been in trouble before
What situation the boy was in when he did it
ask.why: The same shove can be bullying or a desperate defence, depending on what was happening. Rules and past records matter, but without the situation they can lead to an unfair call. Asking about the context first lets her judge the act with nuance.

chapters.take: The same action can mean very different things. Ask about the situation.

story.b: A week later, a few teachers want Devansh suspended. They say understanding his reasons just means excusing him. Rekha disagrees, gently. She does not want him let off. He must apologise to the boy, and he helps the school peon fix the water cooler tap. But she also wants the causes dealt with, so there is no next time. The school counsellor starts meeting Devansh once a week. The boy who mocked his stammer gets his own talk with Rekha. A quiet corner of the library is opened after school, so Devansh has somewhere calm to study. Rekha also meets his parents, not to scold them, but to ask how the school can help.

ask.q: Some staff want Devansh suspended for the fight. What approach fits best?
o: Suspend him, since understanding the causes would only excuse him
Hold him accountable, but focus on understanding the causes and preventing a repeat
Let him off entirely, since his circumstances caused it
ask.why: Pure punishment ignores the causes that will trigger the next fight. Letting him off teaches nothing and leaves others unprotected. Holding him accountable while working on the causes, like the teasing and his broken sleep, protects everyone and gives him a real chance to change.

chapters.take: Understanding causes is not excusing. It is how you prevent the next time.

story.b: By the end of the term, the wooden bench outside Rekha's office is empty more often than it used to be. She has added one line to the school's incident form: what was happening before this? Teachers grumbled at first. Now some of them ask it out loud before they even reach her office. Kabir still fidgets, but he runs errands and asks good questions. The mixed science teams have become a yearly event. Devansh studies in the library corner most afternoons and has started helping two Class 6 boys with their maths. His stammer is still there. The mocking is not. Rekha is still firm. She has simply become curious first.

chapters.take: Curiosity about causes made her firmer, fairer and kinder, all at once.
